summary: Defines jCard, a JSON format for vCard data, which represents information about people and entities such as phone numbers, emails, names and addresses. This makes vCard data easier to use in JSON-based applications.

plainLanguage.summary: jCard is JSON for contact cards. A vCard is a list of lines such as FN:John Doe and TEL;TYPE=work:tel:+1-418-656-9254. RFC 7095 says how each of those lines becomes a JSON array, so that web code can read a contact list without first parsing a text format. The mapping goes both ways, and nothing in the card is lost on the way.

subtitle: How to write an address-book card (vCard) as plain JSON so web code can read it easily.

tldr.problem: vCard is a text format for contact information that is awkward for the JavaScript libraries and widgets used in web applications to parse.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7095 maps every part of a vCard onto JSON: a vCard becomes an array of property arrays, each property holding a name, a parameters object, a type name and one or more values, with dates and times written in the extended ISO 8601 form.
tldr.outcome: Applications can exchange contact data as JSON, and a new UNKNOWN value type lets values survive a round trip even when the converter does not recognise the property. The document registers the media type application/vcard+json and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7095 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the JSON form of the vCard format specified in RFC 6350 and registers the media type application/vcard+json.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The vCard data format defined in RFC 6350 provides for the capture and exchange of information normally stored in an address book or directory application. The format has gone through multiple revisions, most recently vCard 4.

Because of the similarities between vCard and the iCalendar data format in RFC 5545, there is also an effort to define a JSON-based format for calendar information called jCal, which parallels the format defined here. JSON is the JavaScript Object Notation defined in RFC 4627.

The purpose of this document is to define jCard, a JSON format for vCard data. The main advantage over the classic vCard format is easier processing for JavaScript-based widgets and libraries, especially in web applications.

The key design considerations are essentially the same as those for jCal and for xCal in RFC 6321. Converting a vCard instance to jCard and back gives the same semantic result as the starting point, so all components, properties and property parameters are guaranteed to be preserved. The ordering of elements and the case of property and parameter names are not necessarily preserved. The vCard data semantics are preserved, so a simple consumer can browse the data in jCard, although a full understanding of vCard is still required to modify or fully comprehend the directory data. Extensions to the underlying vCard specification must not lead to a need to update jCard.
sections.plainLanguage: jCard exists so that code written for the web can read contact data directly. The format keeps the meaning of every field, keeps every field and parameter through a conversion round trip, and does not need to change when vCard gains new extensions.

sections.title: The jCard Object and Pre-processing
sections.content:
Before anything else, the converter handles the text-level encoding of vCard. vCard folds long lines to keep them to a maximum length, typically 75 octets, so that the data survives transport by means such as email. vCard also uses an escape character sequence for text values and property parameter values. When converting from vCard to jCard, vCard lines must first be unfolded, then any vCard escaping must be unescaped, and finally JSON escaping must be applied. The reverse order applies when converting from jCard to vCard: JSON escaping is unescaped first, then vCard escaping is applied, and finally long lines should be folded.

One key difference in the formatting of values is that jCard uses date and time values aligned with the extended format of ISO 8601, which is more commonly used in Internet applications that use JSON.

In RFC 6350, the BEGIN and END properties delimit a syntactic vCard entity. In jCard, each syntactic entity is represented by an array with two elements, named the jCard object. The first element is the string vcard, and the second element is an array of jCard properties belonging to the entity. Although RFC 6350 defines BEGIN and END as properties, they must not appear as properties of the jCard, because the jCard object is itself enough to define a vCard entity. When converting from jCard to vCard, the BEGIN and END properties must be added to enclose the properties of the jCard object.

Consumers that need several cards in one JSON document can use a simple JSON array whose each element is a single jCard object.
sections.plainLanguage: A vCard starts and ends with BEGIN:VCARD and END:VCARD. In jCard those lines disappear, because the array itself marks the start and end. A card becomes a two-element array: the word vcard, then the list of properties.

sections.title: Properties and Their Special Cases
sections.content:
Each vCard property is represented by an array with three fixed elements, followed by one or more further elements if the property is multi-valued. The first element is the name of the property as a lowercase string, because vCard property names are case insensitive but must be lowercase in jCard. The second element is an object holding the parameters, or an empty object when the property has no parameters. The third element is the type identifier string of the value, in lowercase; parsers must check it rather than rely on assumptions, so for a structured value the type is array.

The remaining elements hold the values of the property. A single-valued property therefore has exactly four elements, while a multi-valued property adds one element per value. A property value may itself be a structured value, in which case it is represented as an array inside the property array; the values inside that array are of the type named by the type identifier. A value inside a structured array may be a further nested array when that component itself has multiple values.

The VERSION property is mandatory in vCard. The jCard version property must be represented in the corresponding jCard component with the same value, and vCards conforming to RFC 6350 carry the value 4.0. The version property must be the first element of the array of properties.

Grouping of related properties is done differently. In vCard, a group name followed by a dot is prefixed to the property name. In jCard, a group parameter holds the group name, and a property name must not be prefixed. Converting from vCard to jCard removes the group construct and puts the group name in the group parameter, whose value is case insensitive and whose case should be converted to lowercase. Converting back prefixes the group name and a dot to the property name and discards the parameter; the GROUP parameter must not appear in the resulting vCard, and the name's case should be converted to uppercase.

Structured property values, such as GENDER or ADR, are text components delimited by semicolons in vCard. In jCard they become an array with one element per text component, with missing components represented by zero-length strings. Some vCard properties, ADR for example, allow a structured element that itself has multiple values, in which case that element is itself an array. The array elements must have the primitive type that matches the type identifier; in RFC 6350 there are only structured text values, so only JSON strings are used, but extensions may define structured number or boolean values. Although a structured property value may hold just one component, it is recommended to represent it as a single text value instead and omit the array, though a simple implementation may keep the array. Similarly, structured values of two text components where one is optional, such as GENDER, can be represented as a single text value, so parsers should check even known property values for structured information by looking at the JSON data type of the value. The component separator must be specified even when the component value is missing, and the jCard array must contain all required elements even if they are empty.
sections.plainLanguage: Each property becomes an array: the name, an object of parameters, the type of the value, and then the value itself. Names are always lowercase. A property that holds several values has one array element for each. A property that holds a compound value, such as a postal address, holds an array of its parts, and missing parts appear as empty strings so that the positions stay right.

sections.title: Parameters
sections.content:
Property parameters are represented as a JSON object in which each key-value pair is one vCard parameter name and its value. The parameter name must be lowercase, while the original case of the parameter value must be preserved, so the LANGUAGE property parameter becomes the language key. Any new vCard parameters added in the future are converted the same way.

The VALUE property parameter must not be added to the parameters object, because the value type is signalled through the type identifier in the third element of the property array. When converting a property from vCard to jCard, the value type is the value of the VALUE parameter if there is one, otherwise the default value type of the property if it has one, and otherwise unknown. When converting from jCard into vCard, no VALUE parameter is included when the value type is unknown or when it is the default type for that property, and otherwise a VALUE parameter is included carrying the value type as its value.

Some vCard parameters allow a comma-separated list of values. In jCard such a parameter must be represented by an array containing the separated values, and the array elements must be strings. Single-value parameters should be represented by a single string, although a simpler implementation might use an array with one string element. The SORT-AS parameter is an example. The vCard specification requires encapsulation between DQUOTE characters when a parameter value contains a colon, a semicolon or a comma; those extra DQUOTE characters are not part of the actual value and are not included when the parameter is converted to jCard.
sections.plainLanguage: Parameters, such as the type of a phone number, become an object with lowercase names. The VALUE parameter is treated differently: instead of appearing in that object, the value type is written into the property array as its own element, so parsers can see the type without looking inside the parameters.

sections.title: Value Types and Date and Time Formats
sections.content:
Each vCard value type maps to a jCard type identifier. Text values use the identifier text and the value elements are JSON strings. URI values use uri, again with JSON strings. Date values use date and are JSON strings with the same date value as in vCard, but written in the extended format of ISO 8601. If the complete representation is not used, the same restrictions on reduced accuracy and truncated representation apply as in RFC 6350, and whenever the extended format does not apply the basic format must be used.

Time values use time. The seconds value of 60 may only be used to account for a positive leap second, and the midnight hour is always represented by 00, never 24. Fractions of a second are not supported. Unlike jCal, UTC offsets are permitted within a jCard time value.

Date-time values use date-time, and follow the same restrictions. Date and/or time values use date-and-or-time, and a stand-alone time value must always be preceded by a T. Timestamp values use timestamp, with the extended and complete representation of ISO 8601.

Boolean values use boolean and the value element is a JSON boolean. Integer values use integer and the value elements are JSON primitive numbers; JSON allows decimals and exponents, which jCard does not prohibit for integer values, but since vCard does not support them, any decimals and exponents must be eliminated when converting to vCard. Float values use float and the same rule applies to exponents. UTC offset values use utc-offset, with the hour and minute components separated by a colon for consistency with the ISO 8601 extended format. Language tag values use language-tag and hold a single language tag as defined in RFC 5646.

Extension properties and parameters, those whose vCard name starts with X-, are handled like any other property, with the name in lowercase, so the vCard property X-FOO becomes the jCard property x-foo.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value in jCard says what kind of value it is, using a short name such as text, uri, date or boolean. Dates and times are written in the long ISO 8601 form, so a birthday is 1985-04-12 rather than 19850412, and a time carries a colon between hours and minutes.

sections.title: Round-Tripping and Unknown Properties
sections.content:
When converting to vCard, property and parameter names should be converted to uppercase, because vCard names are case insensitive and common practice keeps them uppercase. Character escaping and line folding must be applied to the resulting vCard data as required by RFC 6350 and RFC 6868. The VALUE parameter must be added to properties whose default value type is unknown but whose jCard type identifier is not unknown, may be omitted for properties using the default value type, and must be omitted for properties that have the jCard type identifier unknown.

A vCard property can have one or more allowed value types, one of which is the default. When a property uses its default value type, the VALUE parameter need not be given. The BDAY property, for example, has the default value type date-and-or-time, but it also allows a text value, and then VALUE=text has to be set.

A converter may meet a property or parameter it does not recognise, and not know the appropriate default value types, yet it still has to preserve the values. jCard therefore introduces a new unknown property value type whose purpose is to preserve unknown property values during round-tripping. To avoid collisions, the UNKNOWN property value type is reserved in vCard: it must not be used in any vCard as specified by RFC 6350, nor in any extensions to it.

Converting vCard into jCard, any property with no VALUE parameter and no known default value type must be converted to a primitive JSON string holding the unprocessed value text, with the value type set to unknown. It is critical to use unknown in this case, because if the requirement is ignored and, for example, text is used, extra escaping may occur that breaks round-tripping. Any unrecognised property parameter must be converted to a string value holding the parameter value text, treated as if it were a TEXT value.

Converting jCard into vCard, the value type is always explicit, and it is carried by the vCard VALUE parameter, except that the VALUE parameter may be omitted when the jCard value type matches the vCard default, and must not be specified when the jCard value type is unknown, in which case the value is taken over in vCard without processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a converter meets a property it has never seen. jCard has a type called unknown for exactly that case: the value is kept as plain text and passed through untouched, so nothing is lost when the card is written back out as vCard. A converter that used the text type instead would add escape characters and break the value.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines how vCard data is translated between two data formats, the original text format and JSON, with a one-to-one mapping so that all the semantic data in one format are preserved in the other. It does not change the semantic meaning of the underlying data, and it neither imposes nor removes any security considerations that apply to that data.

Using JSON as a format does bring its own inherent security risks, as discussed in Section 7 of RFC 4627. Even though JSON is considered a safe subset of JavaScript, a flaw in the parser for JSON data could still impose a threat that does not arise with conventional vCard data. The parser for JSON data should therefore be aware of the security implications. For example, the use of JavaScript's eval() function is only allowed using the regular expression in Section 6 of RFC 4627, and a native parser with full awareness of the JSON format should be preferred.

The RFC also notes that it is expected this new format will result in vCard data being more widely disseminated, for example with use in web applications rather than just dedicated contact managers. In all cases, application developers have to conform to the semantics of the vCard data as defined in RFC 6350 and its extensions, and all of the security considerations described in Section 9 of RFC 6350, or of any associated extensions, apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The format itself adds no new security rules for contact data. The risk that matters is in the code: a program should parse JSON with a real JSON parser rather than evaluating text as code, because a parser bug becomes a security hole.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a MIME media type for use with vCard in JSON data, which should be used for the transfer of calendaring data in JSON. The type name is application and the subtype name is vcard+json. There are no required parameters; the optional parameter version is defined as for the text/vcard media type in RFC 6350. The encoding considerations are the same as those of application/json as specified in RFC 4627. The intended usage is COMMON and there are no restrictions on where the media type can be used. The change controller is the IETF.

Two registry entries are added. The GROUP parameter is added to the vCard Parameters registry, reserved for the exclusive use of the jCard format; it must not be used in plain vCard or in xCard. Because the value of the GROUP parameter becomes part of the property name when converting to vCard, its value is restricted to ALPHA, DIGIT and hyphen characters, and it must not be empty when used. The UNKNOWN value data type is added to the vCard Value Data Types registry, with the purpose of preserving property values whose default value type is not known during round-tripping between jCard and vCard. It is reserved for the exclusive use of the jCard format and must not be used in plain vCard.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are reserved so that jCard can use them safely. The GROUP parameter and the UNKNOWN value type exist only in jCard, and both are registered so that no future vCard extension can take them and break the mapping.

items.title: Round-tripping
items.text: Converting a vCard to jCard and back gives the same semantic result, so all components, properties and parameters are preserved.

items.title: Ordering
items.text: The order of elements and the case of property and parameter names are not preserved.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: The meaning of the vCard data is preserved, so a simple consumer can browse the data in jCard.

items.title: Extensions
items.text: Extensions to the vCard specification must not require an update to jCard.
